\chapter{Dos grados}
\label{ch:es-abrigo}
\hlchaptermodality{468}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can act on a cold-weather reading: take a temperature in degrees off a bus-stop screen, and choose between a jacket, a coat and a scarf on the strength of the number rather than a general impression.}

Read a bus-stop screen and a message from home, then decide what to put on.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la chaqueta]{la chaqueta — the jacket}

\label{lesson:ES-C468-chaqueta}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el jersey} and \textbf{la piel}. Both lessons put the next word in front of you without stopping to teach it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la chaqueta}
\textbf{la chaqueta} — the jacket.

\begin{quote}
Hace frío. Llévate una \textbf{chaqueta}.
\end{quote}

\emph{Una chaqueta de piel} — a leather jacket, the phrase \emph{la piel} already gave you. \emph{La chaqueta del traje} — the suit jacket.

Among knitwear the line is clean: a \emph{jersey} goes over your head, a \emph{chaqueta de punto} opens down the front — which is what a cardigan is. Beyond knitwear a \emph{chaqueta} is any short tailored jacket.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where} & \textbf{the everyday word} \\
\midrule
Spain & \textbf{la chaqueta} \\
much of Latin America & \textbf{el saco}, \textbf{la campera}, \textbf{la chamarra} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Take the regional column seriously here. In Mexico and much of Central America \emph{chaqueta} carries a vulgar second sense, and the neutral word is \emph{saco} or \emph{chamarra}.

\begin{cousinweb}
You were shown this one in passing when you learned \emph{el jersey}, in a table of garments named after somewhere. It sat there as the odd row, because it is not named after a place at all.

French \textbf{jaquette} is a small \textbf{jaque}, a short tunic — and that much is firm. Where \emph{jaque} came from is not. One account takes it to \textbf{Jacques}, the stock name for a French peasant, the way English once said \emph{Jack} for any ordinary man. Another takes it through Spanish \emph{jaco} to an Arabic word for a mail jerkin. Both are live; neither is proved.

You already know Spanish will name a garment after its wearer — \emph{los vaqueros} are the cowherd's trousers. If the Jacques account is right, \emph{la chaqueta} is the same habit, which is why it sat in the wrong column of the \emph{jersey} chapter's table:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{garment} & \textbf{named after} \\
\midrule
el jersey & an island \\
la chaqueta & a man's name, probably \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English took both ends of the pair: \textbf{jack}, a medieval padded tunic, straight from \emph{jaque}; and \textbf{jacket}, from the little one, \emph{jaquette}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item it's cold, take a jacket
  \item a leather jacket
  \item the word to use instead in Mexico
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The jacket, in Spain? (\textbf{La chaqueta}.) And in Mexico? (\textbf{El saco} or \textbf{la chamarra}.) Who is it probably named after? (\textbf{Jacques} — a peasant's name, on the usual account.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el grado]{el grado — the degree}

\label{lesson:ES-C468-grado}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la temperatura}, then the scale: \emph{poco}, \emph{bastante}, \emph{muy}. The word coming next is what that scale is a scale of, and you have never been given it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el grado}
\textbf{el grado} — the degree.

\begin{quote}
Estamos a tres \textbf{grados}.
\end{quote}

\emph{Doce grados} — twelve degrees. \emph{Bajo cero} — below zero. The everyday frame with a number is \textbf{estar a}: \emph{estamos a tres grados}, we are at three degrees. You will also hear \emph{hace tres grados} and \emph{hay tres grados}; \emph{estar a} is the one to produce.

When you learned \emph{la temperatura} you got the quantity without its unit. This is the unit.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word you already had under another job}]
\emph{Poco}, \emph{bastante}, \emph{muy} is a scale of \textbf{degree}, and \emph{degree} is \textbf{grado}. The review that taught that scale carries this word in its own filename and never once put it in front of you. Here it is.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{use} & \textbf{what it counts} \\
\midrule
\emph{tres grados} & steps up a thermometer \\
the \emph{poco / bastante / muy} scale & steps up a quality \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Latin \textbf{gradus} is a \textbf{step} — the one you take walking. From there it went to any step in a series: a step on a staircase, a step of rank, a step of temperature. English keeps the walking sense in \textbf{gradual}, one step at a time, and in \textbf{grade}, \textbf{degree} and \textbf{graduate}, who has climbed the steps.

So a \emph{grado} is not only a number. It is a position on a set of stairs, and a thermometer is a staircase somebody agreed the height of.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Gradus} also gives Spanish \textbf{el grado} for a university degree and for a school year, and \textbf{la graduación}, which is both the ceremony and the strength of an alcohol — another scale with steps on it.

\textbf{De buen grado} — willingly, gladly — is a different word, from \emph{gratum}, pleasing. Two \emph{grado}s, and only this one has stairs in it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item we're at three degrees
  \item twelve degrees, then below zero
  \item what gradus means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The degree? (\textbf{El grado}.) How do you say it is three degrees? (\textbf{Estamos a tres grados}.) What is a \emph{gradus}? (\textbf{A step}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el abrigo]{el abrigo — the coat}

\label{lesson:ES-C468-abrigo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el frío} and \textbf{la chaqueta}. One is the reason for the next word; the other is not warm enough for it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el abrigo}
\textbf{el abrigo} — the coat, the overcoat.

\begin{quote}
A tres grados no salgas sin \textbf{abrigo}.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Abrigar} is the verb: \emph{abrígate}, wrap up warm. And \emph{una manta que abriga mucho} is a blanket that keeps you very warm — the verb is about the warmth, not the wrapping.

A \emph{chaqueta} is a jacket. An \emph{abrigo} is the long one you put on over everything else when it is properly cold.

\begin{cousinweb}
This word is not named for its shape. It is named for what it does.

Behind \emph{abrigar} is Latin \textbf{apricari}, to \textbf{bask in the sun}. \emph{Apricus} was the adjective: open to the sun, warm.

Then Spanish did something quietly odd with it. A word for a place the sun gets \textbf{into} became a word for a place the weather cannot, and the coat is named for the second one. \emph{El abrigo} is not \textquotedblleft{}a long coat\textquotedblright{}, it is \textbf{a shelter} — \emph{un abrigo rocoso} is a hollow in the rock face out of the weather, and \emph{al abrigo de} is \textbf{in the shelter of}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{the shelter} \\
\midrule
el abrigo & the one you wear \\
al abrigo de & the one you stand behind \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Watch that second one: what follows \emph{de} is what shelters you, not what you are hiding from.

One warning while \emph{apricus} is in front of you: English \textbf{apricot} looks like a relative and is not one. That word came through Arabic and Portuguese from Latin \emph{praecoquum}, the early-ripening fruit, and the resemblance to \emph{apricus} is a coincidence people have been reading meaning into for centuries.

So the garment is named for the sunny corner it replaces.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item at three degrees don't go out without a coat
  \item wrap up warm
  \item what apricari meant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The coat? (\textbf{El abrigo}.) The verb? (\textbf{Abrigar}.) What did \emph{apricari} mean? (\textbf{To bask in the sun} — the coat is a shelter you wear.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la bufanda]{la bufanda — the scarf}

\label{lesson:ES-C468-bufanda}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el abrigo} and \textbf{la chaqueta}. One more goes on top of either, and it is the last piece this chapter needs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la bufanda}
\textbf{la bufanda} — the scarf, the winter one you wind round your neck.

\begin{quote}
Ponte la \textbf{bufanda}, que estamos a dos grados.
\end{quote}

That \textbf{que} is not the joining \emph{que} you have. It is the spoken shorthand for \emph{porque} — \emph{put your scarf on, because it's two degrees} — and Spanish leans on it constantly for reasons.

A \emph{bufanda} is the one you put on because it is cold. \textbf{Un fular} is the light draped one worn for how it looks; \textbf{un pañuelo} is usually a handkerchief and only sometimes a scarf. A \emph{bufanda} can be silk, so the material is not the test — the reason is.

\begin{cousinweb}
Every other word in this chapter came with a story. This one comes with a shrug, and you have met that shrug before.

\emph{La bufanda} has no settled origin. The usual suggestion is French \textbf{bouffante}, puffed out, on \emph{bouffer}, to puff — which fits a scarf's bulk around the throat. Another line points at Italian \emph{buffa}, a visor or a covering for the face. The dictionaries hedge, and so does this lesson.

\emph{El patio} is where this book set the rule out: an origin left open is a claim, not an oversight, and saying so is more useful than picking the prettier story. \emph{El andén}, \emph{tirar} and \emph{el gorro} carry the same mark, and \emph{el gorro} is the nearest neighbour — winter headwear whose origin the Academy also marks uncertain.

\emph{La bufanda} is the fifth. Read the prose rather than the front matter for this: plenty of lessons leave the root list empty and still tell you the whole story. What is unusual here is that there is no story to tell.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item put your scarf on, because it's two degrees
  \item which scarf is for warmth and which is for looks
  \item where la bufanda comes from
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The scarf? (\textbf{La bufanda}.) Where does it come from? (\textbf{Nobody has settled it} — French \emph{bouffante} is the usual guess.) Which earlier word said the same? (\emph{\textbf{El patio}}, or \emph{el gorro}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(la chaqueta, el grado, el abrigo, la …]{(la chaqueta, el grado, el abrigo, la bufanda) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R468-repaso-abrigo}



\begin{quote}
Four words, no prompts. What you put on, what you put on over it, what goes round your neck, and the number that decides.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the four, cold}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
the jacket & \textbf{la chaqueta} \\
the degree & \textbf{el grado} \\
the coat & \textbf{el abrigo} \\
the scarf & \textbf{la bufanda} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a list that was closed, reopened on purpose}]
The wardrobe chapter called its list covered end to end. It was — for what that exam asked. \emph{Pantalón}, \emph{falda}, \emph{camisa}, \emph{zapato}, \emph{vaqueros}, \emph{jersey}, \emph{bolso}: enough to say what you are wearing.

What it could not do is answer a question about \textbf{weather}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the old list} & \textbf{this chapter} \\
\midrule
what you are wearing & what the cold makes you wear \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the difference between the two exams. The first asks you to describe; the second asks you to decide, and deciding needs a number. \emph{Hace frío} was never going to be enough once somebody writes \emph{estamos a dos grados} on a screen at a bus stop.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Two of the four have a settled origin, a third has a guess, and the fourth refuses.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{underneath} \\
\midrule
el grado & \emph{gradus}, a \textbf{step} — a thermometer is a staircase \\
el abrigo & \emph{apricari}, to \textbf{bask in the sun} — a shelter you wear \\
la chaqueta & \emph{Jacques}, a peasant's name — probably \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{La bufanda} has no agreed origin at all, and its lesson says so rather than covering over, the way \emph{el patio} and \emph{el gorro} did before it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item it's two degrees, put a coat and a scarf on
  \item which of the four has no known origin
  \item what a gradus is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The jacket? (\textbf{La chaqueta}.) The degree? (\textbf{El grado}.) The coat? (\textbf{El abrigo}.) The scarf? (\textbf{La bufanda}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(el aviso de la parada) — read it, then decide}

\label{lesson:ES-C468-sintesis-abrigo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el grado} and \textbf{el abrigo}. The first decides the second, which is the whole task here.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
On the screen at the bus stop:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{07:40 — LÍNEA 12 — 6 min}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Ahora: \textbf{2 grados}. Máxima hoy: 7 grados.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{(La máxima is the day's high.)}
\end{quote}

And a message on your phone:

\begin{quote}
Hace mucho frío. Ponte el \textbf{abrigo}, no la \textbf{chaqueta}. Y llévate la \textbf{bufanda}, que estuviste enfermo la semana pasada.
\end{quote}
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the message is doing that the screen cannot}]
The screen gives a number. The message gives a decision, and the two are not the same kind of statement.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the screen} & \textbf{the message} \\
\midrule
\emph{2 grados} & \emph{ponte el abrigo, no la chaqueta} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Note \textbf{no la chaqueta}. With the chosen thing said first, Spanish needs only \emph{no} and the thing ruled out. Turn it round and you are back in the shape \emph{sino} gave you — \emph{no la chaqueta, sino el abrigo}. Same correction, two orders.

And \emph{que estuviste enfermo} gives the reason, with the spoken \textbf{que} that stands in for \emph{porque}, which \emph{la bufanda} introduced two lessons ago. A screen rarely explains itself; a person usually does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say what the temperature is now and what it will reach.

Now answer the message: say what you are putting on and what you are leaving behind, using \emph{no} the way the message does.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How cold is it? (\textbf{Estamos a dos grados}.) What goes on? (\textbf{El abrigo} and \textbf{la bufanda}.) What stays behind? (\textbf{La chaqueta}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
